connection: Session 12 established the prerequisite model. This session applies it to reusable type parameters with observable TimeClock examples.

concept.title: Build the behavioral model
paragraphs: The central rule is that a type parameter lets one checked design preserve compile-time type information for many payload types.
Names and syntax matter because they communicate whether code copies, aliases, enumerates, compares, or constrains a value.

concept.title: Program to the required capability
paragraphs: A caller should not need to provide more capability than the operation consumes.
Concrete implementations remain useful at construction boundaries; interfaces and generic contracts keep consuming code focused.
concept.code:
// Prefer the smallest contract that supports the operation.
Result<decimal> result = Result<decimal>.Success(8m);

concept.title: Verify cause and effect
paragraphs: The lab changes one behavior at a time and uses tests to preserve the observation.
If the prediction differs from the result, explain the language rule before continuing.

lab.objective: Add a focused TimeClock example that demonstrates generic types and methods.
lab.startingCondition: Sessions 01–12 are complete and the solution builds with all existing tests passing.
steps: Read the starting test and predict the result using the session mental model.
Add src/TimeClock.Domain/Result.cs with the smallest API needed for the example.
Add tests/TimeClock.Domain.Tests/ResultTests.cs to check the important before-and-after behavior.
Run the focused tests, then run the complete Release test suite.
Review whether each parameter and return type exposes only the capability it needs.
lab.expectedBehavior: The new tests demonstrate a type parameter lets one checked design preserve compile-time type information for many payload types; all existing behavior remains green.
lab.validation: dotnet build TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

postQuiz.prompt: What did the lab establish about generic types and methods?
options: a type parameter lets one checked design preserve compile-time type information for many payload types
The compiler cannot describe the behavior
Tests replace the need for a mental model
postQuiz.explanation: The test makes the language rule observable and repeatable.

postQuiz.prompt: Why run the entire suite after the focused test?
options: To detect regressions across cumulative code
postQuiz.explanation: The course application grows cumulatively, so earlier guarantees must remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: When should a concrete collection or implementation leak into an API?
options: Only when its specific capability is part of the contract
postQuiz.explanation: Expose concrete capability only when callers genuinely need it.

whatBreaks: Removing the new domain example removes the executable model for reusable type parameters. Removing its tests allows subtle changes to assignment, equality, enumeration, or generic contracts to pass unnoticed. Widening the API unnecessarily gives callers capabilities the operation does not need.
summary: This session established that a type parameter lets one checked design preserve compile-time type information for many payload types. The TimeClock example, tests, and API review turn that rule into durable engineering practice.
